lead: A linear operator is a rule that stretches, rotates or reflects vectors while preserving sums and scalar multiples. Choose a basis and the operator becomes a matrix, so matrix algebra is operator algebra in coordinates. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are the directions the operator does not turn, only scales. This is used wherever a quantum gate, a measurement or a time evolution must be written as a matrix.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for vector spaces over C and 1.3 for bases and Dirac notation.

blocks.text: A linear operator A on a vector space acts on vectors and returns vectors. It is linear when A(αu + βv) = αAu + βAv for all vectors u, v and all scalars α, β. Here α and β are numbers, real or complex. Linearity means the operator respects addition and scaling.

blocks.where: A is a linear operator; u and v are vectors; α and β are scalars.

blocks.text: Fix a basis e1, e2. The matrix of A in this basis has columns equal to the coordinates of A e1 and A e2. For the standard basis e1=(1,0), e2=(0,1), write A = [[a,b],[c,d]]. Then A e1 = (a,c) and A e2 = (b,d). The same operator has different matrices in different bases, but its action on vectors is unchanged.

Use 2×2 matrices in this chapter. A Pauli matrix such as σz = [[1,0],[0,−1]] is a linear operator on C². Its quantum meaning as an observable or a gate belongs to Unit 2 and Unit 3, not here. Some syllabi call this topic matrices and operators.

Matrices of the same size add entry by entry, and a scalar multiplies every entry. Composition of operators becomes matrix multiplication. If C = AB, then (AB)<sub>ij</sub> = Σ<sub>k</sub> A<sub>ik</sub> B<sub>kj</sub>. Here i is the row, j is the column, and k runs over the shared dimension. Matrix product is not commutative in general: AB ≠ BA.

The identity matrix I = [[1,0],[0,1]] satisfies AI = IA = A. An inverse A<sup>−1</sup> exists only when det(A) ≠ 0, and it satisfies AA<sup>−1</sup> = A<sup>−1</sup>A = I. For A = [[a,b],[c,d]], the determinant is det(A) = ad − bc. The inverse is A<sup>−1</sup> = (1/det(A)) [[d,−b],[−c,a]]. If det(A) = 0, A is singular and has no inverse.

blocks.where: A = [[a,b],[c,d]]; a,b,c,d are entries; det(A) is the determinant.

blocks.text: These rules are the same for complex matrices. They let you solve A x = b by x = A<sup>−1</sup>b when the inverse exists.

An eigenvector v of A is a nonzero vector that A only scales: A v = λ v. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue. Rewrite as (A − λI)v = 0. A nonzero solution v exists only when det(A − λI) = 0. This is the characteristic equation. For 2×2 A, it is a quadratic in λ.

blocks.where: A is the operator; v is a nonzero eigenvector; λ is the eigenvalue.

blocks.text: Solve det(A − λI) = 0 for λ. Put each λ back into (A − λI)v = 0 and solve for v. Scale v freely; (2,2) is the same eigenvector as (1,1).

If A has two independent eigenvectors v1, v2 with eigenvalues λ1, λ2, then A = P D P<sup>−1</sup>. Here P has columns v1, v2, and D = diag(λ1, λ2). This is diagonalization. It fails when there are not enough independent eigenvectors, for example a repeated eigenvalue with only one eigenvector.
Eigenvalues reveal the scaling directions of an operator. That is why they matter for quantum measurement and time evolution; see 1.5.

figure.caption: A = [[2,1],[1,2]] has eigen-directions y = x and y = −x. The vector (1,1) stretches to (3,3) with λ = 3; (1,−1) stays fixed with λ = 1.

spec.aria: A plot for A = [[2,1],[1,2]] showing the eigen-direction lines y = x and y = −x; (1,1) is scaled to (3,3) by λ = 3, and (1,−1) is unchanged by λ = 1.

examples.question: Let A = [[2,1],[1,2]]. Find both eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each eigenvalue. Verify A v = λ v for each pair.
examples.answer: The eigenvalues are 3 and 1; eigenvectors are (1,1) for 3 and (1,−1) for 1.
examples.check:
a, b, c, d = 2, 1, 1, 2
tr = a + d
det = a*d - b*c
disc = tr*tr - 4*det
l1 = (tr + disc**0.5)/2
l2 = (tr - disc**0.5)/2
print(int(l1))
print(int(l2))

traps: An eigenvector cannot be the zero vector. v=0 makes Av=λv true for every λ, so it carries no information.
Do not divide by v. Write (A−λI)v=0 and set det(A−λI)=0; v is a vector, not a number.
det(A−λI)=0 gives eigenvalues. Substituting λ back gives eigenvectors; keep the two steps separate.
A repeated eigenvalue may have only one independent eigenvector; then the matrix cannot be diagonalized. Do not assume two eigenvectors.
det(A−λI) is not det(A)−λ. Expand the determinant after subtracting λ from the diagonal entries.

quiz.q: State the definition of a linear operator.
quiz.a: A linear operator A satisfies A(αu+βv)=αAu+βAv for all vectors u,v and all scalars α,β.

quiz.q: Write the eigenvalue equation and state the condition on v.
quiz.a: A v = λ v, where v is a nonzero vector and λ is a scalar eigenvalue.

quiz.q: Why does choosing a basis turn an operator into a matrix?
quiz.a: The columns of the matrix are the coordinates of the images of the basis vectors. Once the basis is fixed, each vector has a coordinate column, and linearity fixes the action on every vector from the action on the basis.
A is upper triangular, so det(A−λI)=(1−λ)(3−λ)=0. The eigenvalues are 1 and 3.

quiz.q: For A = [[0,1],[1,0]], find the eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each.
quiz.a: det(A−λI)=(−λ)(−λ)−1=λ²−1=0, so λ=1 and λ=−1. For λ=1, solve −x+y=0 and x−y=0, giving y=x, so v=(1,1). For λ=−1, solve x+y=0, giving y=−x, so v=(1,−1).

quiz.q: A 2×2 real matrix has trace 4 and determinant 3. Find its eigenvalues and decide whether it is diagonalizable.
quiz.a: λ²−4λ+3=0 gives (λ−3)(λ−1)=0, so λ=3 and λ=1. The eigenvalues are distinct, so there are two independent eigenvectors and the matrix is diagonalizable.

quiz.q: Give a 2×2 matrix with repeated eigenvalue 1 that is not diagonalizable, and explain why.
quiz.a: A = [[1,1],[0,1]] has det(A−λI)=(1−λ)²=0, so λ=1 twice. Solve (A−I)v=0: [[0,1],[0,0]] gives y=0, so only (1,0) up to scaling. One independent eigenvector is not enough for a 2×2 diagonalization.

beyond: Not for the exam. Matrix diagonalization is the same idea behind principal component analysis, where eigenvectors of a covariance matrix give directions of largest variance. In quantum computing, the Pauli matrices are both Hermitian and unitary, so they are observables and gates at once; see Unit 3 for their gate actions. Numerical libraries compute eigenvalues with iterative algorithms for large matrices, not by expanding det(A−λI). Search terms: characteristic polynomial, similarity transform, spectral theorem.
